candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns MALWARE with probability 1.0000, but the supplied n-gram evidence does not show cryptojacking behavior on its own. All 20 top features push toward cryptojacking, but the individual contributions are small and flat, from +0.012705 (CMOVZ MOV) down to +0.005551 (or nor). No single feature dominates. Nineteen of the 20 n-grams have a relative frequency of 0.000000, and 'or nor' is only 0.000046, so none is a prominent part of the code. No function locations are listed for any n-gram, so I cannot tie any pattern to a specific routine. Most of the n-grams are generic compiler-generated x86 sequences: MOV/POP/ADD/SUB/AND/XOR combinations, TEST/CMP followed by conditional jumps, and LEA/CALL. These are common in ordinary software. A few are weakly suggestive of bit-manipulation or branchless-selection code: XOR SHL, XOR XOR, XOR CMOVNZ, CMOVZ MOV, and the XOR/CALL pairs. Such code can appear in hashing or mixing routines, but it also appears in many benign programs, so it is not specific to mining. The evidence contains no mining-specific indicators such as stratum or pool strings, wallet addresses, or identifiable hash-loop functions. The high model probability suggests the overall feature distribution resembles the malware training set, but the evidence shown cannot confirm cryptojacking, so I classify it as low-confidence.
